title: Historical & regional geology I
sub: Lecture 8 · 23 Nov · weekly test at the next lecture + final exam
blurb: Relative and absolute dating, radioactive decay and half-life, the geological time scale, the Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic, cratons and shields, and the supercontinent cycle.
h1: Historical and regional geology I, one step at a time
lede: How do geologists put Earth's history in order and give it numbers? First **dating**: relative dating puts rocks in order, absolute (radiometric) dating gives an age in years. Then **geological time** and how it is divided. Then the **early Earth** (Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic) and the **supercontinent cycle**.
six: **Relative dating** puts events in order: **superposition** (younger on top), **original horizontality**, **lateral continuity**, **cross-cutting** (whatever cuts is younger).
**Absolute dating** = the age in years from **radioactive decay**. **Parent** isotope → **daughter** isotope; **half-life** = time for half of the parent atoms to decay.
Pairs: **U-238 → Pb-206** (4.5 billion yr), **K-40 → Ar-40**, **Rb-87 → Sr-87** for old rocks; **C-14 → N-14** (5,730 yr) only for young events.
Time units **eon > era > period > epoch > age** (geochronology); the rocks formed in them: **eonthem > erathem > system > series > stage** (chronostratigraphy).

Earth ~**4.6 Ga**. **Hadean** 4.6–4 Ga (lava planet, no rocks), **Archean** 4–2.5 Ga (first continental crust, stromatolites, photosynthesis), **Proterozoic** 2.5 Ga–540 Ma (oxygen rise, eukaryotes, multicellular life). **Phanerozoic** from ~540 Ma.
**Supercontinent cycle** = the Wilson cycle repeated: **Kenorland** ~2.7 Ga, **Columbia (Nuna)** ~1.8 Ga, **Rodinia** ~1.0 Ga, **Pannotia** ~600 Ma, **Pangea** ~300 Ma.
must: dating principles, half-life and the eons

questions.q: What is historical geology (palaeogeology)?
questions.answer: Using the principles and methods of geology to reconstruct the geological history of Earth
wrong: The geological study of large-scale regions, combining several disciplines to piece together an area's history
The study of rock layers and their relationships in space and time
Determining the precise age of rocks and events using radiometric techniques
questions.e: Slide 2 definition (Levin & King, The Earth Through Time): the history of the whole Earth. The wrong options are regional geology (one large region), stratigraphy and absolute dating.

questions.q: What is regional geology?
questions.answer: The geological study of large-scale regions, combining several disciplines to piece together an area's history
wrong: Using the principles and methods of geology to reconstruct the geological history of the whole Earth
The study of large-scale plate interactions, from regional to global scale
The study of deformational features in rocks, from outcrop to regional scale
questions.e: Slide 3 definition: one large region and many disciplines. The wrong options are historical geology (the whole Earth), tectonics and structural geology (lecture 7).

questions.q: Which principle says that sedimentary layers get younger upwards?
questions.h: One layer lies on top of the other.
questions.e: Superposition: in undisturbed layers the bottom one is oldest, the top one youngest.

questions.q: Which principle says sedimentary layers were originally laid down flat?
questions.e: So tilted or folded layers must have been deformed later.

questions.q: Which principle says sedimentary layers spread out in all directions until they reach the edge of the basin?
questions.e: That is why the same layer can be matched on both sides of a valley, like in the Badlands.

questions.q: A dike cuts through three sedimentary layers. What does the principle of cross-cutting relationships tell you?
questions.answer: The dike is younger than all three layers
wrong: The dike is older than all three layers
The dike is younger than the bottom layer but older than the top one
The dike is the same age as the middle layer
questions.e: Folds, faults and igneous intrusions are younger than the rocks they cut or deform.

questions.q: In the slide 9 diagram (layers A on top, B, C at the bottom; dike D; fault E), which unit is the OLDEST?
questions.e: C is the lowest sedimentary layer and everything else cuts it or lies on it.

questions.q: In the slide 9 diagram, fault E offsets dike D. Which event is the YOUNGEST?
questions.e: Order: C → B → A → D → E. The fault cuts the dike, so the fault is younger.

questions.q: What is absolute dating?
questions.answer: Determining the precise age using radiometric techniques
wrong: Putting rock layers in order (older or younger) using superposition and cross-cutting
Dividing rocks into biozones by their fossil content
Matching the same layer across a valley by lateral continuity
questions.e: Slide 11: absolute dating gives a number (e.g. 341 ± 3 Ma). Relative dating (superposition, cross-cutting, lateral continuity) only gives an order; biozones are biostratigraphy.

questions.q: Who discovered radioactivity, and when?
questions.e: Becquerel, 1896: the spontaneous decay of radioactive isotopes.

questions.q: In alpha decay, what is ejected from the nucleus?
questions.e: Alpha = helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons), U-238 → Th-234. An ejected electron is beta decay; electromagnetic radiation is gamma.

questions.q: In beta decay, what happens?
questions.answer: A neutron breaks down into a proton and an electron, and the electron is ejected
wrong: A proton breaks down into a neutron and an electron, and the electron is ejected
A neutron breaks down into a proton and an electron, and the proton is ejected
A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons) is ejected from the nucleus
questions.e: Slide 12: the NEUTRON breaks down, the ELECTRON leaves, the new proton stays. C-14 → N-14, so the atomic number goes up by one. A helium nucleus is alpha decay.

questions.q: What are gamma rays in radioactive decay?
wrong: Electrons ejected after a neutron breaks down
The stable daughter at the end of a decay chain
questions.e: Gamma rays come along with alpha or beta decay. Helium nuclei = alpha, electrons = beta.

questions.q: In the slide 12 figure, which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.e: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by aluminium; gamma is only weakened by thick concrete.

questions.q: What is the parent isotope?
wrong: The stable element at the end of a decay chain
The isotope with the longest half-life on the slide
questions.e: Parent = original radioactive element; daughter = decay product. The longest half-life on the slide is Rb-87, which is just one parent among many.

questions.q: What is a half-life?
questions.answer: The time for half of the parent atoms to decay
wrong: The time for all of the parent atoms to decay
The time for half of the daughter atoms to decay
Half of the time a decay chain needs to reach a stable daughter
questions.e: After one half-life 1/2 of the parent is left, after two 1/4, after three 1/8.

questions.q: A rock has gone through 2 half-lives since it formed. How much of the original parent isotope is left?
questions.e: 100 % → 50 % → 25 %. 75 % is how much has DECAYED, not what is left. Three half-lives would leave 12.5 %.

questions.q: What is a decay chain?
questions.answer: A series of radioactive parents and daughters that ends with a stable daughter
wrong: A series of stable daughters that ends with a radioactive parent
A single decay step in which a parent turns straight into a stable daughter
A series of rock layers whose order is set by superposition
questions.e: Example from the slide: U-238 → … → Pb-206 (stable).

questions.q: What is the stable daughter of uranium-238?
questions.e: U-238 → Pb-206, half-life 4.5 billion years. (U-235 → Pb-207.)

questions.q: Potassium-40 decays to which daughter?
questions.e: K-40 → Ar-40, half-life 1.25 billion years.

questions.q: Why is carbon-14 used only for young events?
wrong: Its half-life is long: 4.5 billion years
Its half-life is long: 1.25 billion years
Its half-life is long: 704 million years
questions.e: C-14 half-life: 5,730 years, so almost nothing is left after a few tens of thousands of years. 4.5 billion = U-238, 1.25 billion = K-40, 704 million = U-235: those are for old events.

questions.q: Which pair on the slide has the LONGEST half-life?
questions.e: Rb-87: 48.8 billion years. U-238: 4.5 billion. K-40: 1.25 billion. U-235: 704 million. C-14: 5,730 years.

questions.q: Who said "The present is the key to the past" and "No vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end"?
questions.e: Hutton, Siccar Point, Scotland. Processes we see today worked the same way in the past, over immense time.

questions.q: At Siccar Point, what is the unconformity (the red line on slide 17)?
questions.answer: A hiatus: a period of non-deposition or active erosion between two rock sequences
wrong: A fault: a planar fracture along which displacement has occurred
An igneous dike that cut across both rock sequences after they formed
A bedding plane where deposition carried on without a break
questions.e: Below: vertical Silurian ocean rocks (~425 Ma). Above: tilted Devonian desert rocks (~345 Ma). The surface between them is the unconformity: a gap in time, not a fault, dike or normal bedding plane.

questions.q: Why did Charles Darwin need deep geological time?
questions.answer: To explain the evolution of species
wrong: To date rocks using radioactive decay
To explain how continents merge into supercontinents
To explain the principle of superposition
questions.e: Slide 18: Darwin needed deep time to explain the evolution of species. Radioactivity was only discovered in 1896 (Becquerel).

questions.q: What is the correct order of geochronological units, from largest to smallest?
questions.e: Eon > era > period > epoch > age.

questions.q: Which chronostratigraphic unit matches the geochronological PERIOD?
questions.e: Eon–eonthem, era–erathem, period–system, epoch–series, age–stage.

questions.q: Which epoch are we living in now?
questions.e: Quaternary period = Pleistocene, then Holocene (since ~10 ka on the slide).

questions.q: What is stratigraphy?
questions.answer: The study of rock layers and their relationships in space and time
wrong: Determining the precise age of rocks using radiometric techniques
Using geological methods to reconstruct the history of the Earth
The geological study of large-scale regions using several disciplines
questions.e: Slide 20 definition. The wrong options are absolute dating, historical geology and regional geology.

questions.q: Which kind of stratigraphy is based on rock type (lithology), with units like formation, member and group?
questions.e: Litho = rock. Bio = fossils (biozone). Chrono = relative time (system, series, stage).

questions.q: Biostratigraphy divides rocks by …
questions.e: Slide 20 table: bio = fossils (biozone). Rock type = lithostratigraphy, radiometric ages = geochronology, relative time = chronostratigraphy.

questions.q: How old is the Earth?
questions.e: ~4.6 Ga. (13.8 billion years is the age of the universe.)

questions.q: When did the Phanerozoic begin?
questions.e: ~540 Ma, at the start of the Cambrian. Everything before is the Precambrian.

questions.q: What does "Ma" mean?
wrong: Millions of years after the Earth formed
questions.e: Ga = billions, Ma = millions, ka = thousands of years ago.

questions.q: According to the slide, when did life first appear?
questions.e: First emergence of life: >3.5 Ga, in the Archean.

questions.q: According to the nebular theory, how did the Earth form?
questions.answer: From a rotating cloud of gas and dust: the Sun formed in the centre, the planets in orbit
wrong: From a rotating cloud of gas and dust: the planets formed in the centre, the Sun in orbit
From a rotating cloud of gas and dust about 540 Ma, at the start of the Phanerozoic
From material thrown off the Sun after a collision with another star, about 4.6 Ga
questions.e: Nebular theory, ~4.6 Ga. HL Tauri is an example of a young star with a protoplanetary disk.

questions.q: Which eon is described as a "lava planet" with no rocks preserved, only very rare zircons?
questions.e: Hadean, 4.6–4 Ga: differentiation into core, mantle and crust; cooling, degassing, likely oceans by the end.

questions.q: What happened during differentiation in the Hadean?
questions.answer: The Earth separated into core, mantle and crust
wrong: The continents merged into the first supercontinent, Kenorland
The first continental crust and stromatolites appeared
Oxygen rose after the first photosynthesis
questions.e: Differentiation: heavy material sank to form the core, lighter material rose. Kenorland (~2.7 Ga), the first continental crust and stromatolites, and the first photosynthesis all came later, in the Archean.

questions.q: In which eon did the first continental crust and the first microbial life (stromatolites) appear?
questions.e: Archean, 4–2.5 Ga: first continental crust, stromatolites, first photosynthesis.

questions.q: What are stromatolites?
questions.answer: Layered structures built by microbial mats; the first microbial life
wrong: The first eukaryotic cells, from the Proterozoic eon
Very rare zircon crystals preserved from the Hadean
The first multicellular life of the late Proterozoic
questions.e: They formed in the Archean and still grow today in a few places (present-day stromatolites, slide 27).

questions.q: Which eon saw the first eukaryotic cells and the first multicellular life?
questions.e: Proterozoic, 2500–540 Ma: continents grow, modern plate tectonics, oxygen rise, eukaryotes, multicellular life.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the eons, from oldest to youngest?
questions.e: H-A-P-P: Hadean 4.6–4 Ga, Archean 4–2.5 Ga, Proterozoic 2.5 Ga–540 Ma, Phanerozoic 540 Ma–today.

questions.q: On the slide 28 map, what lies at the cores of today's continents?
questions.answer: Archean cratons, surrounded by Proterozoic shields and younger Phanerozoic orogens
wrong: Phanerozoic orogens, surrounded by Proterozoic shields and older Archean cratons
Proterozoic shields, surrounded by Archean cratons and younger Phanerozoic orogens
Archean orogens, surrounded by Proterozoic cratons and younger Phanerozoic shields
questions.e: Continents grew outwards around very old Archean cores.

questions.q: What is a craton?
questions.answer: The old (Precambrian), stable core of a continent
wrong: A mountain belt formed by tectonic convergence
A crustal block with a history different from the rocks around it
A subsiding area where sediments accumulate
questions.e: Craton = old, stable core. The wrong options are orogen, terrane and basin. Shield = exposed craton; platform = craton covered by younger sediments.

questions.q: What is a shield?
questions.answer: The exposed part of a craton, with Precambrian basement at the surface
wrong: A craton covered by younger, mostly sedimentary rocks
Older crystalline rocks underlying younger sedimentary cover
A mountain belt formed by tectonic convergence
questions.e: Shield = exposed craton. Platform = covered craton. Basement = the older crystalline rocks under the cover. Orogen = mountain belt.

questions.q: A craton covered by younger, mostly sedimentary rocks is called a …
questions.e: Platform = covered craton.

questions.q: What is a terrane?
questions.answer: A crustal block with a geological history different from the rocks around it
wrong: The old (Precambrian), stable core of a continent
Older crystalline rocks underlying younger sedimentary cover
A subsiding area where sediments accumulate
questions.e: Terranes get attached to continents, often during collisions. The wrong options are craton, basement and basin.

questions.q: What is an orogen?
questions.answer: A mountain belt formed by tectonic convergence
wrong: The exposed part of a craton
questions.e: Orogen = mountain belt (lecture 7: continental collision).

questions.q: What is the supercontinent cycle?
questions.answer: The repetition of the Wilson cycle: all continents merge into one and then break up again
wrong: The repetition of the rock cycle: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form again and again
The repetition of the eons: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic conditions return
The break-up of Pangea about 300 Ma, which created today's dispersed continents
questions.e: Supercontinents form and break up again and again over hundreds of millions of years.

questions.q: When did Pangea exist?
questions.e: Pangea ~300 Ma. Rodinia ~1.0 Ga, Pannotia ~600 Ma, Kenorland ~2.7 Ga.

questions.q: What is the correct order of supercontinents, from oldest to youngest?
What does the slide say about the future?
questions.answer: There will probably be another supercontinent
wrong: The continents will stay dispersed as they are today
Rodinia will re-form from today's continents
questions.e: Today the continents are dispersed; in the future they will probably merge again.

vocab.meaning: Also palaeogeology. Uses the principles and methods of geology to reconstruct the geological history of Earth.
The geological study of large-scale regions, combining several disciplines to piece together an area's history.
Putting rocks and events in order (older or younger) without giving an age in years.
Principle: sedimentary layers get younger upwards.
Principle: sedimentary layers were originally deposited horizontally.
Principle: sedimentary layers spread laterally in all directions until they hit the edge of the basin.
Principle: folds, faults and igneous intrusions are younger than the rocks they deform or cut across.
Determining the precise age in years using radiometric techniques.
The spontaneous decay of radioactive isotopes. Discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896.
Decay in which a helium nucleus is ejected, e.g. U-238 → Th-234.
A neutron breaks down into a proton and an electron; the electron is ejected, e.g. C-14 → N-14.
Electromagnetic radiation that accompanies radioactive decay.
The original radioactive element.
The product of radioactive decay.
The time it takes for half of the parent atoms to decay.
A series of radioactive parents and daughters that ends in a stable (non-radioactive) daughter, e.g. U-238 → Pb-206.
The immense timescales over which geological processes operate ("deep time").
Divides time itself: eon, era, period, epoch, age. Also the absolute dating of rocks, e.g. 341 ± 3 Ma.
Divides rocks by the relative time they represent: eonthem, erathem, system, series, stage.
A surface between two rock sequences that marks a hiatus: a period of non-deposition or active erosion. Example: Siccar Point, Scotland.
The study of rock layers and their relationships in space and time.
Stratigraphy based on rock type (lithology). Units: formation, member, group.
Stratigraphy based on fossil content. Unit: biozone.
The largest unit of geological time, e.g. Archean, Phanerozoic. Matching rock unit: eonthem.
The present epoch of the Quaternary period, since ~10 ka (slide 21).
A unit of geological time inside an era, e.g. Jurassic. Matching rock unit: system.
The Solar System formed ~4.6 Ga from a rotating cloud of gas and dust: the Sun in the centre, the planets in orbit.
Eon 4.6–4 Ga. "Lava planet"; differentiation into core, mantle and crust; no rocks, only very rare zircons.
Eon 4–2.5 Ga. First continental crust, first microbial life (stromatolites), first photosynthesis.
Eon 2500–540 Ma. Continents grow, modern plate tectonics, oxygen rise, first eukaryotes and multicellular life.
Eon from ~540 Ma to today: Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras.
A layered structure built by microbial mats; among the oldest evidence of life (Archean), still forming today.
The old (Precambrian), stable core of a continent.
The exposed part of a craton; Precambrian basement at the surface.
A craton covered by younger, mostly sedimentary rocks.
Older crystalline rocks underlying younger sedimentary cover.
Younger sediments or sedimentary rocks deposited over the basement.
A mountain belt formed by tectonic convergence.
A crustal block with a geological history distinct from the surrounding rocks.
A subsiding area where sediments accumulate.
The repetition of the Wilson cycle: all continents merge into one and then break up again.
Supercontinent at ~1.0 Ga.
The most recent supercontinent, ~300 Ma.

facts: Historical geology is also called {palaeogeology|petrology|mineralogy|geomorphology}.
Regional geology studies {large-scale regions|single crystals|the inner core|the atmosphere} and combines several geological disciplines.
By the principle of superposition, sedimentary layers get {younger|older|thicker|harder} upwards.
By the principle of original horizontality, sedimentary layers were first deposited {horizontally|vertically|folded|at 45°}.
Sedimentary layers spread laterally until they hit the edge of the {basin|mantle|craton|fault}.
A fault, fold or intrusion is {younger|older|the same age|always 1 Ma older} than the rocks it cuts.
In the slide 9 diagram the youngest event is the {fault E|dike D|layer A|layer C}.
In the slide 9 diagram the oldest unit is {layer C|layer A|dike D|fault E}.
Radioactivity was discovered by {Henri Becquerel|James Hutton|Charles Darwin|Marie Tharp} in 1896.
In alpha decay a {helium|hydrogen|carbon|lead} nucleus is ejected.
In beta decay a neutron breaks down into a proton and an {electron|alpha particle|neutrino only|helium nucleus}, which is ejected.
Beta radiation is stopped by {aluminium|paper|nothing|air}.
The half-life is the time for {half|all|a quarter|a tenth} of the parent atoms to decay.
After three half-lives, {12.5 %|25 %|33 %|0 %} of the parent isotope is left.
Uranium-238 decays to the stable daughter {lead-206|lead-207|argon-40|strontium-87}.
The half-life of uranium-238 is about {4.5 billion years|5,730 years|704 million years|48.8 billion years}.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of {5,730 years|4.5 billion years|1.25 billion years|704 million years}, so it dates only young events.
Potassium-40 decays to {argon-40|nitrogen-14|lead-206|strontium-87}.
"The present is the key to the past" was said by {James Hutton|Charles Darwin|Henri Becquerel|Alfred Wegener}.
Hutton's famous unconformity is at {Siccar Point, Scotland|the Badlands, USA|Barrandovská skála, Prague|the Grand Canyon}.
Darwin needed deep time to explain the {evolution of species|age of the Moon|radioactive decay|ice ages}.
At Siccar Point the lower, vertical rocks were deposited in a deep {ocean|desert|lake|glacier} about 425 Ma.
An unconformity marks a hiatus: a period of non-deposition or active {erosion|folding|volcanism|metamorphism}.
The geochronological units from largest to smallest are eon, era, {period|age|stage|system}, epoch, age.
The rock unit that matches a period is a {system|series|stage|erathem}.
The rock unit that matches an epoch is a {series|system|stage|eonthem}.
The Mesozoic era contains the Triassic, Jurassic and {Cretaceous|Permian|Devonian|Neogene} periods.
The Carboniferous is split into the Mississippian and the {Pennsylvanian|Permian|Devonian|Silurian}.
Lithostratigraphy is based on {rock type|fossils|absolute ages|magnetism} and uses formations, members and groups.
The unit of biostratigraphy is the {biozone|formation|stage|eon}.
The Earth is about {4.6|2.5|13.8|0.54} billion years old.
The Phanerozoic began about {540|66|2,500|4,000} million years ago.
The abbreviation {Ga|Ma|ka|BP} means billions of years ago.
According to the nebular theory, the Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of {gas and dust|water and ice|molten iron|granite}.
The Hadean eon lasted from 4.6 to {4|2.5|3.5|0.54} Ga.
From the Hadean no rocks survive, only very rare {zircons|stromatolites|fossils|diamonds}.
Degassing during the Hadean produced the early {atmosphere|core|crust|continents}.
The first continental crust formed in the {Archean|Hadean|Proterozoic|Phanerozoic} eon.
The first microbial life is recorded by {stromatolites|trilobites|ammonites|dinosaur bones}.
The first eukaryotic cells appeared in the {Proterozoic|Archean|Hadean|Phanerozoic}.
The Proterozoic eon ended about {540|2,500|4,000|66} million years ago.
A craton is the old, stable, {Precambrian|Cenozoic|Jurassic|Quaternary} core of a continent.
A craton covered by younger sedimentary rocks is a {platform|shield|terrane|orogen}.
A crustal block with a history different from its surroundings is a {terrane|craton|basin|platform}.
A subsiding area where sediments accumulate is a {basin|shield|orogen|craton}.
The supercontinent cycle is the repetition of the {Wilson|rock|carbon|water} cycle.
Rodinia existed about {1.0 Ga|300 Ma|2.7 Ga|600 Ma}.
The oldest supercontinent on the slide is {Kenorland|Rodinia|Pangea|Pannotia}, about 2.7 Ga.
Columbia is also called {Nuna|Gondwana|Laurasia|Baltica}.
